claim: Advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is associated with a poor prognosis.
source: Advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and biomarkers that predict response to treatment are highly desirable.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Experimental covariates were derived from blood samples of 56 HNSCC patients which were prospectively obtained within a Phase 2 clinical trial (NCT02633800) at baseline and after the first treatment cycle.
source: Experimental covariates were derived from blood samples of 56 HNSCC patients which were prospectively obtained within a Phase 2 clinical trial (NCT02633800) at baseline and after the first treatment cycle of combined platinum-based chemotherapy with cetuximab treatment.
evidence: This describes the study design and data collection methodology.

claim: A baseline risk prediction model was generated featuring clinical and experimental covariates.
source: A 'baseline' and a 'combined' risk prediction model were generated, each of which featuring clinical and experimental covariates.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's findings.

claim: The baseline risk signature has three covariates and was strongly driven by baseline percentage of CD33+CD14+HLADRhigh monocytes.
source: The baseline risk signature has three covariates and was strongly driven by baseline percentage of CD33+CD14+HLADRhigh monocytes.
evidence: This describes the composition and key driver of the baseline model based on the analysis.

claim: The combined signature has six covariates, featuring baseline CD33+CD14+HLADRhigh monocytes but is strongly driven by on-treatment relative change of CD8+ central memory T cells percentages.
source: The combined signature has six covariates, also featuring baseline CD33+CD14+HLADRhigh monocytes but is strongly driven by on-treatment relative change of CD8+ central memory T cells percentages.
evidence: This describes the composition and key driver of the combined model based on the analysis.

claim: The combined model has a higher predictive power than the baseline model.
source: The combined model has a higher predictive power than the baseline model and was successfully validated to predict therapeutic response in an independent cohort of nine patients from an additional Phase 2 trial (NCT03494322) assessing the addition of avelumab to cetuximab treatment in HNSCC.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about model performance based on the study's analysis.

claim: The combined model was successfully validated to predict therapeutic response in an independent cohort of nine patients from an additional Phase 2 trial (NCT03494322).
source: The combined model has a higher predictive power than the baseline model and was successfully validated to predict therapeutic response in an independent cohort of nine patients from an additional Phase 2 trial (NCT03494322) assessing the addition of avelumab to cetuximab treatment in HNSCC.
evidence: This describes the validation of the model in an independent cohort.

claim: Tissue counterparts for the immune cells driving the models were identified using imaging mass cytometry that specifically colocalized at the tissue level and correlated with outcome.
source: We identified tissue counterparts for the immune cells driving the models, using imaging mass cytometry, that specifically colocalized at the tissue level and correlated with outcome.
evidence: This describes findings from imaging mass cytometry analysis.

claim: For many years, the standard-of-care first-line systemic treatment was the EXTREME regimen, consisting of a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen and cetuximab, an anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody.
source: For many years, the standard-of-care first-line systemic treatment was the EXTREME regimen, consisting of a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen and cetuximab, an anti-EGFR monoclonal antibody (Van Cutsem et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Van Cutsem et al., 2009.

claim: The KEYNOTE-048 trial in 2019 changed the treatment paradigm for HNSCC patients by incorporating pembrolizumab into the first-line setting.
source: The KEYNOTE-048 trial in 2019 changed the treatment paradigm for these patients by incorporating pembrolizumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, into the first-line setting (Burtness et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burtness et al., 2019.

claim: The EXTREME regimen remains a first-line standard-of-care for patients with PD-L1 negative tumours or those with contraindications to anti-PD1 immunotherapy.
source: However, the EXTREME regimen remains a first-line standard-of-care for a substantial number of patients, specifically those with programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) negative tumours or those with contraindications to the use of anti-PD1 immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as current clinical practice knowledge.

claim: Efforts to generate biomarkers in HNSCC have focused on gene expression profiles, which are dependent on the availability of tumour tissue and are only performed on pre-treatment samples.
source: Until the development of PD-L1 as a biomarker for immunotherapy, efforts to generate biomarkers in HNSCC have focused on gene expression profiles, which are dependent on the availability of tumour tissue and are only performed on pre-treatment samples (Bossi et al., 2016; You et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bossi et al., 2016 and You et al., 2019.

claim: Signatures based on a single biological modality and taken at a single timepoint may be insufficient to predict outcomes.
source: Signatures based on a single biological modality and taken at a single timepoint may be insufficient to predict outcomes, as response to therapy relies on a dynamic interplay between cancer genomics, immune profile, tumour microenvironment, and clinicopathological characteristics of the patient receiving treatment (Cheerla and Gevaert, 2019; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheerla and Gevaert, 2019 and Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Efforts to develop a machine learning model to stratify survival risk by combining genetic and clinicopathological characteristics have revealed some success in advanced oral squamous cell carcinoma.
source: Efforts to develop a machine learning model to stratify survival risk by combining genetic and clinicopathological characteristics have revealed some success in advanced oral squamous cell carcinoma (Tseng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tseng et al., 2020.

claim: Eighty-seven patients were enrolled in the clinical trial NCT02633800.
source: Eighty-seven patients were enrolled in the clinical trial.
evidence: This describes the study enrollment.

claim: Thirty-one patients were excluded due to incomplete paired biological datasets, leaving 56 patients for analysis.
source: Thirty-one patients were excluded due to incomplete paired biological datasets, leaving 56 patients for analysis.
evidence: This describes the final study cohort after exclusions.

claim: There was no difference in PFS between patients who received patritumab and those who did not.
source: Amongst these patients, there was no difference in PFS as demonstrated by Kaplan-Meier survival curve analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) regardless of whether the patients received patritumab, which reflected the results published in the clinical trial.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no significant difference between the clinicopathological characteristics pertaining to the discovery cohort and the whole cohort of study.
source: The baseline clinical characteristics of these 56 patients are shown in Supplementary file 1 together with a comparison that shows there is no significant difference between the clinicopathological characteristics pertaining to the discovery cohort and the whole cohort of study.
evidence: This is based on comparison analysis shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: PBMC samples were analysed using flow cytometry to generate unique immunological subpopulations.
source: PBMC samples were analysed using flow cytometry to generate unique immunological subpopulations.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Exosomes were extracted from the serum and analysed for EGFR-ErbB3 dimerization and miRNA-21-5p and miRNA-142-3p.
source: Exosomes were extracted from the serum and analysed for EGFR-ErbB3 dimerization and miRNA-21-5p and miRNA-142-3p (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the methodology and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: These analyses yielded a total of 29 unique biological covariates.
source: These analyses yielded a total of 29 unique biological covariates.
evidence: This describes the number of covariates generated from the analyses.

claim: Each covariate was obtained in pairs (C1 and C2), generating a total of 58 laboratory-based covariates for the multivariate analysis.
source: Each covariate was obtained in pairs (C1 and C2), generating a total of 58 laboratory-based covariates for the multivariate analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the total number of covariates used in the analysis.

claim: The baseline clinical characteristics and laboratory-based covariates did not significantly differ between the placebo and patritumab cohorts.
source: The baseline clinical characteristics, as well as value of the laboratory-based covariates at baseline and after one cycle of treatment, did not significantly differ between the placebo and patritumab cohorts (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on comparison analysis shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: Samples from both the control and investigational arms were analysed together in the exploratory analysis.
source: Therefore, in this exploratory analysis, samples from both the control and investigational arms were analysed together.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach taken in the study.

claim: Bayesian multivariate proportional hazards regression was used to rank and select covariates by predictive importance.
source: Using Bayesian multivariate proportional hazards regression, covariates were ranked and selected by predictive importance (Grigoriadis et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology used, supported by citation to Grigoriadis et al., 2018.

claim: A baseline predictive model was derived containing a dataset of 42 baseline covariates (29 laboratory parameters at baseline and 13 clinical characteristics).
source: We derived two models using separate datasets: firstly, a baseline predictive model containing a dataset of 42 baseline covariates (29 laboratory parameters at baseline (C1) and 13 clinical characteristics).
evidence: This describes the composition of the baseline model.

claim: A combined predictive model consists of 71 covariates, including the 42 baseline covariates and 29 derived from on-treatment changes.
source: The second, a combined predictive model, consists of 71 covariates, that is, the 42 baseline covariates and a further 29 derived from the on-treatment change of the value of a lab-based parameter relative to its value in the same patient at baseline denoted as lfc of that variable.
evidence: This describes the composition of the combined model.

claim: The relative efficiency of the predictive model was assessed using C-index and rank correlation of the signature-generated risk scores with survival time.
source: The relative efficiency of the predictive model was assessed by using C-index (a metric proposed by Harrell et al., 1984, to evaluate the accuracy of predictions made by an algorithm) and rank correlation of the signature-generated risk scores with survival time.
evidence: This describes the evaluation metrics used, with citation to Harrell et al., 1984.

claim: Systematic iterative covariate rejection and cross-validation (5000 iterations) allowed for the selection of an optimal covariate set to avoid overfitting.
source: Systematic iterative covariate rejection and cross-validation (5000 iterations) allowed for the selection of an optimal covariate set to avoid overfitting though inclusion of too many covariates.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to prevent overfitting.

claim: Proportional hazards regression revealed two baseline immune subpopulations (CD33+CD14+ monocytes and double negative B cells) and one clinical covariate (age) with β values exceeding the critical threshold.
source: This revealed two baseline immune subpopulations with a β value which exceeded the critical β value threshold, that is, CD14+CD16+CD33+CD11b+ monocytes thereafter referred to as CD33+CD14+ monocytes according to previous nomenclature (Cravens et al., 2007) and double negative (CD27-IgD-) B cells (DN B cells), as well as one clinical covariate – age (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the results of the proportional hazards regression analysis, shown in Figure 2B, with citation to Cravens et al., 2007.

claim: Baseline CD33+CD14+ monocytes have a β value of –1.05, indicating higher baseline values predict better PFS.
source: Evaluation of the individual β values reveal that baseline CD33+CD14+ monocytes and DN B cells have a β value of –1.05 and –0.53, respectively, and hence a higher baseline value of both populations is predictive of better PFS.
evidence: This describes the specific β values and their interpretation from the analysis.

claim: DN B cells have a β value of –0.53, indicating higher baseline values predict better PFS.
source: Evaluation of the individual β values reveal that baseline CD33+CD14+ monocytes and DN B cells have a β value of –1.05 and –0.53, respectively, and hence a higher baseline value of both populations is predictive of better PFS.
evidence: This describes the specific β values and their interpretation from the analysis.

claim: Age has a β value of 0.47 and is associated with poorer PFS.
source: Age, with a β value of 0.47, is associated with poorer PFS.
evidence: This describes the specific β value for age and its interpretation.

claim: The baseline risk scores correlated strongly with PFS (C-index=0.60, τ=−0.33, p=0.0005).
source: The baseline risk scores correlated strongly with PFS (C-index=0.60, τ=−0.33, p=0.0005).
evidence: This provides specific statistical measures of the baseline model's performance.

claim: The median PFS of the low-risk and high-risk cohorts based on baseline signature are 8.3 and 3.6 months, respectively (log rank p-value = 6.0e-5).
source: The median PFS of the low-risk and high-risk cohorts are 8.3 and 3.6 months, respectively (log rank p-value = 6.0e-5).
evidence: This provides specific survival outcomes for risk-stratified groups.

claim: Six covariates were identified in the combined model: baseline CD33+CD14+ monocytes, baseline CD4+ memory regulatory T cells, increase in CD8+ effector memory T cells, increase in CD8+ central memory T cells, increase in CD3 T cells, and hypopharyngeal primary tumour site.
source: A total of six covariates were identified – three immune subpopulations with negative β values and hence associated with better survival, that is, baseline CD33+CD14+ monocytes, baseline CD4+ memory regulatory T cells (HLA-DR-CD45RO+Tregs), and an increase in CD8+ effector memory T cells (CD45RO+CCR7-). An increase in two subpopulations, CD8+ central memory T cells (CD45RO+CCR7+) and CD3 T cells, was associated with inferior PFS. The hypopharyngeal primary tumour site was also associated with a poorer PFS (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This describes the covariates identified in the combined model analysis, shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: The combined risk scores exhibited a stronger correlation with PFS than the baseline risk scores (C-index=0.69, τ=−0.49, p=7e-7).
source: The combined risk scores exhibited a stronger correlation with PFS than the baseline risk scores (C-index=0.69, τ=−0.49, p=7e-7).
evidence: This provides specific statistical measures comparing the combined model to the baseline model.

claim: In the combined predictive signature, the median PFS of the low-risk and high-risk cohorts are 6.8 and 3.6 months, respectively (log rank p-value 0.004).
source: In this combined predictive signature, the median PFS of the low-risk and high-risk cohorts are 6.8 and 3.6 months, respectively (log rank p-value 0.004) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This provides specific survival outcomes for risk-stratified groups based on the combined model, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The difference in EGFR-ErbB3 FRET (FRET.delta) was associated with a negative β value suggesting better PFS, but fell marginally short of featuring in the eventual predictive signature.
source: In Figure 3A (fourth covariate from the bottom), the difference in EGFR-ErbB3 FRET (FRET.delta) was associated with a negative β value which suggests a better PFS. However, the stringency that we have applied to optimal covariate selection means that this covariate fell marginally short of featuring in the eventual predictive signature.
evidence: This describes a covariate that showed a trend but did not meet the stringent selection criteria, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Patients with a high FRET.delta exhibited a trend toward better PFS than patients with a low FRET.delta, though this difference was not statistically significant (log rank p-value = 0.2).
source: By dividing the patients with available FRET values by the median FRET.delta (n=43), there was a suggestion that patients with a high FRET.delta exhibited a better PFS than patients with a low FRET.delta. This difference was not statistically significant (log rank p-value = 0.2) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes a non-significant trend observed in the data, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A significant correlation was identified between the log fold changes of miR-21-5p and the corresponding log fold changes of CD33+CD14+ monocytes (r=0.43, p=0.02).
source: By correlating the miRNA changes in our study with this monocytic subpopulation, a significant correlation was identified between the log fold changes of miR-21-5p with the corresponding log fold changes of CD33+CD14+ monocytes (r=0.43, p=0.02, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a correlation analysis result shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The validation cohort consisted of 16 patients from the EACH trial (NCT03494322).
source: The validation cohort of 16 patients was obtained from the EACH trial (NCT03494322) which evaluated the combination of avelumab with cetuximab in HNSCC patients.
evidence: This describes the validation cohort source.

claim: PBMCs were successfully obtained from eight patients at the pre-treatment timepoint and after one cycle of cetuximab in the validation cohort.
source: As the risk signature consisted predominantly of immune subpopulations, we successfully obtained PBMCs from eight patients at the pre-treatment timepoint and after one cycle of cetuximab hence matching the timepoints of the original cohort.
evidence: This describes the sample collection for the validation cohort.

claim: In the original test cohort, patient PFS data strongly and inversely correlated with BOR (τ=−0.52, p=3e-6).
source: We confirmed that in the original test cohort, patient PFS data strongly and inversely correlated with BOR (τ=−0.52, p=3e-6) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes a correlation analysis result shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The combined risk signature strongly correlated with a poorer treatment outcome in the validation cohort (τ=0.73, p=0.02).
source: The combined risk signature strongly correlated with a poorer treatment outcome (τ=0.73, p=0.02) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the validation result shown in Figure 5B.

claim: High pre-treatment levels of CD33+CD14+monocytes significantly correlated with a worse disease outcome in the validation cohort.
source: High pre-treatment levels of CD33+CD14+monocytes significantly correlated with a worse disease outcome in all patients except for a single outlier who exhibited a complete response to treatment.
evidence: This describes a finding from the validation cohort analysis.

claim: A post-treatment increase in CD8+ central memory cells (lfcCD8CM) correlated with a poorer treatment outcome in the validation cohort.
source: A post-treatment increase in CD8+ central memory cells (lfcCD8CM) also correlated with a poorer treatment outcome.
evidence: This describes a finding from the validation cohort analysis.

claim: Baseline CD33+CD14+ monocyte levels showed a modest split in PFS that reached significance (log rank p-value = 0.03).
source: We observed a modest split that reached significance only in the case of baseline CD33+CD14+ monocyte (log rank p-value = 0.03) and not in the case of lfcCD8CM cells (log rank p-value = 0.1).
evidence: This describes univariate analysis results in the original cohort.

claim: lfcCD8CM more strongly predicted PFS (C-index=0.74, τ=−0.36, p=0.01) than baseline CD33+CD14+ monocytes (C-index=0.39, τ=0.22, p=0.07).
source: lfcCD8CM more strongly predicted PFS (C-index=0.74, τ=−0.36, p=0.01) than base line CD33+CD14+ monocytes (C-index=0.39, τ=0.22, p=0.07).
evidence: This provides comparative predictive performance of two covariates.

claim: CD14+CD16+CD33+CD11b+ monocytes also express high levels of HLA-DR.
source: Due to the consistency with which the CD33+CD14+ monocyte population appeared across our study, we wanted to further characterize this population to determine its phenotype hence we expanded the antibody panel for the validation set and determined that these CD14+CD16+CD33+CD11b+ monocytes also express high levels of HLA-DR (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes additional characterization of the monocyte population shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sufficient tissue from the biopsy at trial enrolment for in-depth profiling by imaging mass cytometry was obtained from nine patients.
source: We obtained sufficient tissue from the biopsy at trial enrolment for in-depth profiling by imaging mass cytometry from nine patients.
evidence: This describes the tissue sample availability for imaging mass cytometry.

claim: None of the superpopulations identified by imaging mass cytometry correlated with PFS.
source: The distribution of the superpopulations per patient is shown in Figure 6B, yet none of which correlated with PFS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a negative finding from the imaging mass cytometry analysis, shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The peripheral intermediate monocyte population strongly correlated with a tissue CD14+CD33+CD74+CD68+ macrophage population.
source: The peripheral intermediate monocyte population strongly correlated with a tissue CD14+CD33+CD74+CD68+ macrophage population while the CD8CM inversely correlated with CD45RO+CD27+CD8+ tissue resident memory T cell (CD8Trm) population.
evidence: This describes a correlation between peripheral and tissue immune populations.

claim: CD8CM inversely correlated with CD45RO+CD27+CD8+ tissue resident memory T cell (CD8Trm) population.
source: The peripheral intermediate monocyte population strongly correlated with a tissue CD14+CD33+CD74+CD68+ macrophage population while the CD8CM inversely correlated with CD45RO+CD27+CD8+ tissue resident memory T cell (CD8Trm) population.
evidence: This describes an inverse correlation between peripheral and tissue immune populations.

claim: Both CD14+CD33+CD74+CD68+ macrophages and CD8Trm populations positively correlated with PFS.
source: Both of those populations positively correlated with PFS.
evidence: This describes the relationship between tissue immune populations and outcome.

claim: The peripheral CD33+ monocyte population strongly correlated with CD8Trm.
source: Interestingly, the peripheral CD33+ monocyte population strongly correlated with CD8Trm (Figure 6D).
evidence: This describes a correlation shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CD8Trms were significantly more likely to be in contact with a CD74+ macrophage than any other identified population.
source: We found these cells were significantly more likely to be in contact with a CD74+ macrophage than any other identified population suggesting this interaction is biologically driven and not random (Figure 6E).
evidence: This describes cell-to-cell interaction analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The 5-year relative survival of patients with hypopharyngeal SCC is consistently the worst amongst different anatomical HNSCC sub-sites.
source: This corroborates previous findings that the 5-year relative survival of patients with hypopharyngeal SCC is consistently the worst amongst different anatomical HNSCC sub-sites (Gatta et al., 2017; Machiels et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gatta et al., 2017 and Machiels et al., 2020.

claim: Hypopharyngeal tumours have a propensity to present at the de novo advanced stage.
source: The propensity of hypopharyngeal tumours to present at the de novo advanced stage (Cadoni et al., 2017) and the density of submucosal lymphatics in this anatomical region translates into these patients inherently performing worse – lending support to the robust nature of our predictive signature.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cadoni et al., 2017.

claim: The absence of patritumab in the predictive signatures is consistent with the outcome of the Phase 2 clinical trial where the addition of this investigational medicinal product did not produce any benefit to PFS.
source: The notable absence of patritumab (denoted as 'Drug') in our predictive signatures is also consistent with the outcome of the Phase 2 clinical trial where the addition of this investigational medicinal product did not produce any benefit to PFS (Forster et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Forster et al., 2019.

claim: There is a high level of inter-individual heterogeneity in the relative abundance of PBMC subpopulations even between healthy donors.
source: There is a high level of inter-individual heterogeneity in the relative abundance of PBMC subpopulations even between healthy donors.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about PBMC populations.

claim: The combined risk signature had higher predictive power than the baseline one due to presenting biological data as change relative to baseline.
source: By opting to present the biological data obtained from the first post-treatment biopsy as change relative to the baseline biopsy, we obtained a much more predictive risk signature in our combined model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the performance of the two models.

claim: The post-treatment change in CD8CM percentage relative to baseline value is the strongest predictor of PFS in the combined model.
source: This is highlighted in the post-treatment change in CD8CM percentage relative to baseline value which is not only the strongest predictor of PFS in the combined model, but also has a greater univariate predictive value than the whole baseline signature.
evidence: This describes the relative importance of a specific covariate in the combined model.

claim: The risk signature was validated across different treatment modalities (targeted therapies in the first trial and anti-EGFR plus anti-PD-L1 therapy in the second).
source: The fact that the first trial involved targeted therapies and the second a combination of anti-EGFR and anti-PD-L1 therapy, yet the same blood kinetic change can still distinguish between responders and non-responders is novel and has not been seen before according to our knowledge.
evidence: This describes the novelty of the validation across different treatment regimens.

claim: None of the univariates identified in the test cohort independently predicted treatment outcome in the validation cohort.
source: This further highlights the power of multivariate analysis as none of the univariates identified in the test cohort independently predicted treatment outcome in the validation cohort, yet the risk signature strongly correlated with a poorer outcome.
evidence: This describes the limitation of univariate analysis compared to multivariate analysis.

claim: The peripheral CD33+HLADR+ monocytes correspond to a similar population of CD74+CD68+ tumoural myeloid cells.
source: These correlated with a similar population of CD74+CD68+ population of tumoural myeloid cells.
evidence: This describes the relationship between peripheral and tissue immune populations.

claim: The peripheral CD33+CD14+CD16+HLADRhigh monocyte population and the CD14+CD33+CD74+CD68+ tissue macrophages represent the same group of cells that gain CD68 expression as they enter the tissue.
source: Given the similarity in the marker expression patterns between the peripheral CD33+CD14+CD16+HLADRhigh monocyte population and the CD14+CD33+CD74+CD68+ tissue macrophages, as well as the strong correlation between their corresponding blood and tissue abundance (Figure 6D), we hypothesize that they represent the same group of cells that gain CD68 expression as they enter the tissue.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on marker expression patterns and correlation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The monocyte population matches the population of intermediate monocytes described in the literature shown to have a key role in antigen presentation.
source: This monocyte population matches the population of intermediate monocytes described in the literature shown to have a key role in antigen presentation (Cravens et al., 2007; Zawada et al., 2011; Wong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cravens et al., 2007; Zawada et al., 2011; and Wong et al., 2011.

claim: The myeloid population may induce post-treatment expansion of CD8CM potentially via a mechanism involving cross-presentation of antigens released by drug-induced cancer cell death.
source: Given the correlation between tissue levels CD8+ memory T cell, peripheral intermediate monocytes, and the tissue colocalization of the CD8+ memory T cells with the CD74+ macrophages, we can imagine a role for our myeloid population in inducing post-treatment expansion of CD8CM potentially via a mechanism involving cross-presentation of antigens released by drug-induced cancer cell death (Colbert et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to Colbert et al., 2020.

claim: Cetuximab treatment can be a source of tumour-derived antigens as it has been shown to increase TCR diversity in peripheral T cells as well as cross-presentation by antigen-presenting cells.
source: Indeed, cetuximab treatment can be a source of tumour-derived antigens as it has been shown to increase TCR diversity in peripheral T cells as well as cross-presentation by antigen-presenting cells (Kansy et al., 2018; Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kansy et al., 2018 and Srivastava et al., 2013.

claim: Monocyte-derived macrophages have been shown to activate and expand tissue resident memory T cells (Trm).
source: Nevertheless, monocyte-derived macrophages have been shown to activate and expand tissue resident memory T cells (Trm) (Snyder et al., 2021; Low et al., 2020; Muntjewerff et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Snyder et al., 2021; Low et al., 2020; Muntjewerff et al., 2020; and Chu et al., 2020.

claim: An on-treatment increase in the level of circulating CD8CM significantly correlated with a worse disease outcome in patients who received two regimens of systemic treatments within two trials.
source: An on-treatment increase in the level of circulating CD8CM significantly correlated with a worse disease outcome in patients who received two regimens of systemic treatments within two trials.
evidence: This describes a consistent finding across two trials.

claim: High levels of pre-treatment CD8CM cells correlating with a favourable treatment outcome in HNSCC has been previously and independently reported by the Whiteside group.
source: Interestingly, high levels of pre-treatment CD8CM cells correlating with a favourable treatment outcome in HNSCC has been previously and independently reported by the Whiteside group indirectly validating our results (Czystowska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Czystowska et al., 2013.

claim: Tumour reactive T cell clones can be found in the periphery, as proven by single-cell sequencing and mapping of T cell receptor clonality.
source: Using single-cell sequencing and mapping of T cell receptor clonality at the levels of TILs and peripheral T cells, researchers have definitively proven that tumour reactive T cell clones can be found in the periphery (Fairfax et al., 2020; Kok et al., 2020; Pauken et al., 2021; Padrón et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fairfax et al., 2020; Kok et al., 2020; Pauken et al., 2021; and Padrón et al., 2022.

claim: There is continuous recruitment of memory T cells from the periphery into the tumour which replenishes the pool of tissue Trm identified by CD103 and TCF1 expression.
source: The movement of these cells between the tumour and draining lymph node was recently investigated using photoactivable T cells in mice which showed that there is continuous recruitment of memory T cells from the periphery into the tumour which replenishes the pool of tissue Trm identified by CD103 and TCF1 expression.
evidence: This describes findings from a mouse study about T cell trafficking.

claim: Recruitment of memory T cells into tumours is usually matched by an egress of Trm cells out of the tumour to the draining lymph nodes which is accompanied by decreased expression CXCR6.
source: However, this recruitment is usually matched by an egress of Trm cells out of the tumour to the draining lymph nodes which is accompanied by decreased expression CXCR6 (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: CD8CM are capable of homing into the inflamed tissue and undergoing transcriptional reprogramming to a stable Trm phenotype.
source: The peripheral origin of Trm cells is still under investigation with recent data suggesting that CD8CM are not only capable of homing into the inflamed tissue but also undergoing transcriptional reprogramming to a stable Trm phenotype (Matos et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matos et al., 2022.

claim: The predictive power of the population of peripheral CD8CM stems from its ability to home to the tumour and contribute to the Trm population.
source: We hypothesize that the predictive power of the population of peripheral CD8CM stems from its ability to home to the tumour and contribute to the Trm population which has recently been identified as key player in anti-tumour immunity in HNSCC as well as other cancers mainly in the context of immunotherapy but also in chemo/radiotherapy (Han et al., 2021; Ida et al., 2021; Savas et al., 2018; Djenidi et al., 2015; Luoma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Han et al., 2021; Ida et al., 2021; Savas et al., 2018; Djenidi et al., 2015; and Luoma et al., 2022.

claim: Trm has been identified as a key player in anti-tumour immunity in HNSCC as well as other cancers mainly in the context of immunotherapy but also in chemo/radiotherapy.
source: We hypothesize that the predictive power of the population of peripheral CD8CM stems from its ability to home to the tumour and contribute to the Trm population which has recently been identified as key player in anti-tumour immunity in HNSCC as well as other cancers mainly in the context of immunotherapy but also in chemo/radiotherapy (Han et al., 2021; Ida et al., 2021; Savas et al., 2018; Djenidi et al., 2015; Luoma et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2021; Ida et al., 2021; Savas et al., 2018; Djenidi et al., 2015; and Luoma et al., 2022.

claim: The accumulation of clonally expanded memory T cells in the periphery in poor responders is the potential result of tumour-induced T cell exclusion.
source: The accumulation of clonally expanded memory T cells in the periphery in poor responders is the potential result of tumour-induced T cell exclusion which we can infer from the negative correlation observed between peripheral and tumour infiltrating memory T cells (Jerby-Arnon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Jerby-Arnon et al., 2018.

claim: CD8+ memory T cells are being generated only in patients having a large pre-treatment pool of competent APCs yet these anti-tumour CD8+ memory cells cannot enter the tumour from the periphery hence accumulating in circulation.
source: In this model CD8+ memory T cells are being generated only in patients having a large pre-treatment pool of competent APCs yet these anti-tumour CD8+ memory cells cannot enter the tumour from the periphery hence accumulating in circulation.
evidence: This is a proposed model to explain the observed data.

claim: The lack of Trm-specific markers such as CD103, CD69, and TCF1 from the imaging mass cytometry panel contributed to the anti-correlation between peripheral CD8CM and tissue Trm not being stronger.
source: Unfortunately, one key shortcoming of our study is the lack of Trm-specific markers such as CD103, CD69, and TCF1 from the imaging mass cytometry panel of antibodies which we believe contributed to this anti-correlation not being stronger.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a study limitation and its potential impact.

claim: The combination of biomarkers established prospectively by liquid biopsies early in the treatment course offers potential for the provision of personalized treatments to patients.
source: The present study shows that the combination of biomarkers established prospectively by liquid biopsies early in the treatment course offers potential for the provision of personalized treatments to patients (Nenclares et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings, supported by citation to Nenclares et al., 2021.

claim: Identifying complex biological interplay as having a role in disease outcome is impossible without multivariate analysis.
source: Identifying such complex biological interplay as having a role in disease outcome is impossible without multivariate analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the necessity of multivariate analysis based on the study's approach and findings.

claim: miR-21-5p and miR-142-3p have previously demonstrated prognostic and predictive utility.
source: We also incorporated the analysis of two circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) from exosomes: miR-21-5p and miR-142-3p, which have previously demonstrated prognostic and predictive utility (Summerer et al., 2015; Vahabi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Summerer et al., 2015 and Vahabi et al., 2021.

claim: The ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes (NLR) in the peripheral blood of HNSCC patients prior to treatment has been extensively investigated for its ability to predict disease outcome.
source: The ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes (NLR) in the peripheral blood of HNSCC patients prior to treatment has been extensively investigated for its ability to predict disease outcome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Two meta-analyses identified that a high pre-treatment NLR correlated with worse OS with respective HRs of 1.69 (95% CI: 1.47–1.93; p<0.001) and HR of 1.78 (95% CI: 1.53–2.07; p<0.0001).
source: Two recent meta-analyses on the subject have identified that a high pre-treatment NLR correlated with worse OS with respective HRs of 1.69 (95% CI: 1.47–1.93; p<0.001) and HR of 1.78 (95% CI: 1.53–2.07; p<0.0001) (Mascarella et al., 2018; Takenaka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mascarella et al., 2018 and Takenaka et al., 2018.

claim: Using the combined risk signature, disease outcome was predicted more accurately across two separate treatment modalities than using NLR.
source: Using our combined risk signature, we were able to predict disease outcome more accurately across two separate treatment modalities.
evidence: This is an implicit comparison to the NLR results mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: PD-L1 expression levels, when used in isolation, have not been sufficiently predictive at identifying patients who would benefit from immune checkpoint blockade.
source: Other recent biomarker research has focused on predicting response to immune checkpoint blockade by analysing tissue-based biomarkers, such as PD-L1 expression levels, but when used in isolation have not been sufficiently predictive at identifying patients who would benefit (Burtness et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Burtness et al., 2019.

claim: The biology of HNSCC and likelihood of response to treatment is likely to be dictated by an interplay between tumour immunity, genomic signatures, and a host of clinicopathological characteristics which can only be assessed by a multivariate analysis.
source: While unimodal biomarkers may offer some predictive value, the biology of HNSCC and likelihood of response to treatment is likely to be dictated by an interplay between tumour immunity, genomic signatures, and a host of clinicopathological characteristics which can only be assessed by a multivariate analysis.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the complexity of HNSCC biology.

claim: The ability to extract predictive biomarkers from a blood-based liquid biopsy mitigates certain limitations posed by tissue biopsies.
source: The ability to extract predictive biomarkers from a blood-based liquid biopsy mitigates certain limitations posed by tissue biopsies – particularly the tissue accessibility, technical expertise to obtain the biopsy, patient frailty, and the amount of tissue available.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the advantages of liquid biopsies.

claim: PBMCs offer a much more systemic snapshot of the immune response which overcomes intra-tumoural heterogeneity that results in non-uniform distribution of biomarkers.
source: Moreover, PBMCs offer a much more systemic snapshot of the immune response which overcomes intra-tumoural heterogeneity that results in non-uniform distribution of biomarkers.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the advantages of using PBMCs.

claim: This study is one of the first examples of integrating multiple biological covariates derived from peripheral blood and patient clinical data to generate a signature which predicts treatment response and that has been validated across multiple therapeutic modalities.
source: To our knowledge, the current study is one of the first examples of integrating multiple biological covariates derived from peripheral blood and patient clinical data to generate a signature which predicts treatment response and that has been validated across multiple therapeutic modalities.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study approach.

claim: The combination of analyses (cross-validation iterations, overfitting correlation protocols, corrections for informative data missingness, and probabilistic covariate removal) has been shown to produce robust signatures that do generalize to uncaptured data.
source: This combination of analyses has been shown to produce robust signatures that do generalize to uncaptured data (Barber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barber et al., 2020.
